planting.note: Root stem cuttings in warm, humid conditions and pot into a loose, well-drained mix; this New Guinea shrub-type species wants bright but indirect light to bring out its pink-spotted bronze foliage.

directions: Begonia serratipetala is a shrubby New Guinea species prized for its dark bronze, toothed leaves marked with raised pink spots, the serration repeated along the edges of its small pink flower clusters. Grow it in bright, filtered light with moderate to high humidity, since direct sun scorches the thin leaves while deep shade dulls the spotting and reduces flowering. Let the top layer of a chunky, fast-draining mix dry slightly between waterings to avoid stem and root rot. Pinch growing tips periodically to keep the naturally sprawling cane-type growth bushy rather than leggy.

planting.note: Take stem-tip cuttings and grow on in a hanging basket or shallow pan with a free-draining mix; trailing stems need partial shade and steady moisture to avoid scorching or dropping leaves.

directions: Begonia limmingheiana is a trailing Brazilian species with small, glossy, blue-green leaves spotted white above and flushed purple beneath, grown mainly for hanging baskets and elevated containers. Clusters of coral to orange-red flowers appear in cooler months, giving it value as winter color when many other begonias are resting. Site it in bright, dappled shade and keep the fast-draining mix evenly moist, since the thin trailing stems wilt quickly if the soil dries out completely. Pinch back cascading stems occasionally to encourage branching and a fuller basket.
sources: Clemson Cooperative Extension, Growing Begonias Indoors

planting.note: Divide offsets from the rhizomatous base and pot into a rich, humus-heavy mix; this Central American species needs generous room and steady shade to support its oversized leaves.

directions: Begonia popenoei is a rhizomatous species from the cloud forests of Guatemala and Honduras, grown as a dramatic foliage specimen for its smooth, apple-green leaves that can span close to a foot across on an upright, hosta-like plant. White flowers appear above the foliage but the main appeal is scale and texture rather than bloom. Give it deep, even shade and consistent moisture in rich, well-drained soil, since both drought and intense light quickly mar the broad leaf surface. Because of its size it works best as a focal point in a shaded bed or large container rather than a mixed planting.
sources: Kew Royal Botanic Gardens, Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Root stem-cane cuttings in a humid propagation case, then pot into a rich, airy mix; the thick jointed stems benefit from staking as they mature.

directions: Begonia egregia is a tall, thick-caned species from Brazil grown for its sturdy, bamboo-like jointed stems and broad, glossy leaves rather than for showy flowers. It tolerates fairly deep shade but grows more densely with a few hours of bright, filtered light each day. Keep the rich, well-drained soil evenly moist and provide high humidity, since the large leaves can brown at the edges in dry indoor air. As canes age and lose lower leaves, cut them back hard to force fresh basal growth and keep the plant full.
sources: Kew Royal Botanic Gardens, Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Divide the short rhizome into rooted sections and grow on in a humid terrarium or enclosed case; the hairy leaf surface is prone to spotting if splashed with water.

directions: Begonia olsoniae is a compact rhizomatous species from the coastal forests of southeastern Brazil, grown for its softly hairy, dark green leaves traced with pale lime veining. It prefers deep, warm shade and consistently high humidity, making it well suited to a terrarium or other enclosed, protected setting rather than open room air. Water from below or along the soil surface to keep moisture off the fuzzy leaf blades, which can mark or rot if kept damp. Its low, clumping habit pairs well with other small rhizomatous begonias in a shaded collector's planting.
sources: Kew Royal Botanic Gardens, Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Root short stem cuttings in a sealed, humid propagation box; this New Guinea species is slow to establish and needs consistently high humidity and warmth to thrive.

directions: Begonia bipinnatifida is a small New Guinea shrub species notable for its finely divided, fern-like leaf blades on wiry, dark red stems, a distinctive texture among rhizomatous and shrub-type begonias. It is naturally a plant of hot, humid rainforest understory and performs best in an enclosed terrarium or greenhouse setting where humidity and warmth stay consistently high rather than in typical open-room conditions. Keep it in partial shade on a chunky, fast-draining mix, and avoid letting the soil dry out fully between waterings. Because it is slow-growing and sensitive to dry air, treat it as a specialist collector's plant rather than a casual houseplant.
sources: Kew Royal Botanic Gardens, Plants of the World Online
